w: A self-taught local archaeologist named Basil Brown, digging for landowner Edith Pretty in 1938, uncovered an undisturbed Anglo-Saxon ship burial packed with gold fittings, a ceremonial helmet and Byzantine silver -- treasure fit for the king it likely honors, Raedwald of the East Angles, echoing the world of Beowulf.
s: The ship burial that rewrote Anglo-Saxon history.
_facts: Two Anglo-Saxon cemeteries, 6th-7th century
Undisturbed ship burial found 1938 by Basil Brown for Edith Pretty
Artefacts include gold dress fittings, ceremonial helmet, sword, lyre, Byzantine silver
Likely burial of Raedwald, first king of the East Angles
Compared to the world of Beowulf

w: Torn down by Henry II after a rebellion in 1173, its replacement broke with convention -- no central keep, just a curtain wall ringed by thirteen towers. King John besieged it in 1216; the Howards later filled it with pleasure gardens and meres before debt forced its sale, and in 1636 it passed to a Cambridge college.
s: A castle built with no keep at all.
_facts: Earlier castle destroyed by Henry II after 1173-74 revolt
Rebuilt with 13 mural towers and no central keep
Besieged and taken by King John in 1216
Home of the Mowbray and Howard families with pleasure gardens and artificial meres
Given to Pembroke College, Cambridge in 1636

w: Henry II raised this keep between 1165 and 1173 to plant royal power on a coast the crown didn't fully control, giving it a design unlike any other English castle -- probably borrowed from Byzantine architecture. Historians still call it one of the most remarkable keeps in the country, standing watch over Orford Ness.
s: A castle keep modeled on Byzantium.
_facts: Built 1165-1173 by Henry II
Unique design possibly based on Byzantine architecture
Described by historian R. Allen Brown as one of the most remarkable keeps in England
Views over Orford Ness

w: John Tollemache began building this moated Tudor manor in 1480 -- and remarkably, his descendants still own it more than five centuries on. The house, its moat and its Grade I-listed gardens have stayed in one family's hands, a rare case of unbroken continuity in the Suffolk countryside.
s: One family's home since 1480, moat and all.
_facts: Moated manor house begun by John Tollemache in 1480
Owned by the Tollemache family ever since
Grade I listed house, park and gardens

w: Built in 1923 to disguise a water tower as a weatherboarded cottage, this folly seems to float above the treeline of Thorpeness village. Anti-aircraft fire accidentally hit its tank in the Second World War; when mains water made it redundant in 1977, the tank was removed and the shell converted into an actual house.
s: A water tower disguised as a floating cottage.
_facts: Water tower built 1923, disguised as weatherboarded house
Hit by anti-aircraft gunfire in WWII
Made redundant 1977, tank removed 1979
Converted into five-bedroom house, 85 steps, ~70ft high
Grade II listed since 1995

w: This fortified manor passed from the Wingfields to the de la Poles, who rose to Earls then Dukes of Suffolk on the strength of it -- until a forced surrender of the title in 1493. Henry VIII revived the dukedom in 1514 for Charles Brandon, a Wingfield kinsman who lived here with his wife Mary Tudor.
s: The manor behind three Dukes of Suffolk.
_facts: Grade I listed fortified manor house
Ancestral home of the Wingfield and de la Pole families
De la Poles became Earls then Dukes of Suffolk, surrendered dukedom 1493
Dukedom revived 1514 for Charles Brandon, who lived there with wife Mary Tudor

w: Brewing cask ale on this spot since 1872, Adnams has become as much a fixture of Southwold's identity as the pier or the beach huts. It has since branched out with the Copper House distillery, turning out gin, vodka and whisky alongside the beer that made the name.
s: The brewery that built Southwold's identity.
_facts: Regional brewery founded 1872 by George and Ernest Adnams
Produces cask ale and bottled beers, ~85,000 barrels a year
Copper House distillery established 2010 for gin, vodka and whisky

w: Commissioned in 1890, this lighthouse nearly burned down six days into service when its original oil lamp caught fire. It survived, was automated in 1938, and still stands squarely in the middle of the town rather than out on a headland -- guiding ships 24 nautical miles out with its modern 180-watt lamp.
s: A lighthouse built into the middle of town.
_facts: Trinity House lighthouse, commissioned 1890
Survived a lamp fire six days after commissioning
Automated and electrified 1938
Stands in the centre of Southwold
Range of 24 nautical miles

n: Church of St Michael the Archangel, Framlingham
w: Beneath this Grade I-listed church lie generations of the Howard family, the Dukes of Norfolk whose castle looms over the same market town. The tombs make it one of the grander parish churches in Suffolk -- a resting place for a dynasty as much as a place of worship.
_facts: Church of England church dedicated to St Michael
Burial site of the Howard family
Grade I listed since 1966

w: Built in the neo-Gothic style during the 19th-century Catholic revival, this Ipswich parish church was met with open hostility -- anti-Catholic riots broke out soon after it was completed. It has served the town centre's Catholic community ever since, a survivor of the backlash that greeted it.
s: A church that opened to rioting mobs.
_facts: Neo-Gothic Roman Catholic parish church
Built during the 19th-century British Catholic revival
Target of anti-Catholic riots soon after completion

w: Once private land held by a succession of noble families, this rolling parkland was bought by Ipswich council in 1894 and opened as the town's first public park a year later. At its southern gate stands Christchurch Mansion, a Tudor house that now doubles as a free museum and art gallery.
s: Ipswich's first public park, with a Tudor mansion.
_facts: Historic parkland near Ipswich town centre
Bought by Ipswich Borough Council 1894, opened as first public park 1895
Tudor house Christchurch Mansion holds a public museum and art gallery

w: One of Suffolk's 38 surviving round-tower churches -- and the only one in the county where the tower stands apart from the church entirely, a 12th-century stump watching its 13th-century neighbor across the churchyard. Inside, ledger slabs of the Rabett and Nelson families pave the ground before the altar.
s: Suffolk's only detached round church tower.
_facts: 13th-century church with separate 12th-century round tower
One of 38 round-tower churches in Suffolk, the only detached example
Ledger slabs of the Rabett and Nelson families before the altar
Grade I listed

w: Stranded at the end of a lane beside a moated farmhouse, this redundant medieval church is one of roughly 40 round-tower churches scattered across Suffolk. No longer used for worship, it survives under the Churches Conservation Trust, isolated among the cluster of villages known collectively as The Saints.
s: A round-tower church stranded among The Saints.
_facts: Redundant Anglican church, Grade I listed
One of ~40 round-tower churches in Suffolk
Stands isolated beside moated Church Farm
Cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust

w: Before the bitterns and marsh harriers, this stretch of reed bed and heath held an ancient abbey and a Tudor gun battery -- then farmland, deliberately flooded in WWII to deter a German landing. The RSPB has managed it since 1947, and its eight hides now draw birders chasing rarities like the bittern and the nightjar.
s: Flooded to deter invasion, now a birders' mecca.
_facts: 1,000-hectare RSPB reserve managed since 1947
Site of an ancient abbey and Tudor artillery battery before reclamation
Marshes deliberately flooded in WWII as invasion defence
Managed for bittern, stone-curlew, marsh harrier, nightjar, nightingale
Eight bird hides, within Suffolk Coast and Heaths AONB
